transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name], and I'll be speaking with you today. What brings you in to see me?

Hi, um… I’m here because flying has started to feel way scarier than it should. Like, even just thinking about getting on a plane now makes my stomach kind of drop, and I immediately picture this really bad turbulence from my honeymoon flight. I know, logically, people fly safely every single day, and I can tell myself that over and over, but it doesn’t really stop my mind from going right back to that moment. It’s just gotten to where the idea of flying feels bigger and more frightening than I think it should be.
Is this level of fear or anxiety something you experience in other situations, or does it seem to be mostly limited to flying?

It’s mostly flying. I mean, I don’t feel that same level of fear just going about normal life or being in other places. It’s really tied to the thought of getting on a plane. Like even before anything is actually happening, just imagining boarding or sitting there and waiting for takeoff, my mind goes straight back to that honeymoon flight and the turbulence, and then it feels way more frightening than I know it probably should.

I can talk myself through it a little, like, “People fly every day, planes are safe,” all of that, but it doesn’t really land emotionally. It’s not like every situation makes me feel that way—it’s very specifically flying that sets off that reaction for me.
When you start feeling anxious about flying, does your heart race, do you feel short of breath, or does it feel like a panic attack is coming on?

Yeah, kind of—when it hits, it’s very immediate. Like if I’m just looking up flights for a work conference, I can be totally fine beforehand, and then the second I see the options or start imagining the actual trip, my chest tightens. It’s this sudden rush of panic, like I need to close the laptop right away or get away from the thought before it gets worse.

Even hearing a plane overhead can do it sometimes, which feels embarrassing to say because I know I’m not even on the plane, nothing is happening to me in that moment. But my body reacts before I can really talk myself down. It’s not always some huge scene, but it definitely feels like this wave of fear starting up really fast.
Do you find yourself avoiding flying entirely because of this fear, or have you tried to endure it despite feeling really anxious?

Yeah… I’ve definitely been avoiding it more than I want to admit. It’s not like I’ve completely structured my whole life around never flying, but when there’s a choice, I pick the option that doesn’t involve a plane. Like I’ve chosen these really long drives instead, even when flying would obviously make more sense and save a ton of time.

And with work, that’s been one of the more frustrating parts. If there are trainings or conferences that would require flying, I’ve found myself kind of looking for reasons not to go, or just turning them down. I’ll tell myself it’s because of scheduling or because it’s not essential, but if I’m being honest, the flying part is usually the thing underneath it.

If I absolutely have to talk about a trip—like actually look at flights or make a plan—I have a really hard time doing it by myself. I usually need my husband sitting there with me, just kind of being present and helping me not back out immediately. It feels silly because it’s just a conversation or a website at that point, but without him there I’m much more likely to shut it down and say, “Never mind, I can’t do this.”
How long have you been feeling this way about flying? Has this fear been present for months, or even longer?

It’s been… honestly, since that flight coming back from my honeymoon. That was about two years and five months ago now, which sounds strange to say because it feels both like a long time and also like I can remember it really clearly.

Before that, I wouldn’t say I loved flying, exactly, but it wasn’t like this. The fear really started after that turbulent flight on the way home, and it’s just kind of stayed with me since then. So yes, definitely longer than a few months—over two years at this point.

When you're not actively thinking about flying or planning a trip, do you still find yourself being more aware of things related to planes—like paying extra attention to news about flights, or feeling on edge when you hear a plane overhead?

Yeah, I do notice it, even when I’m not actively planning anything. It’s like planes kind of catch my attention more than they used to. If I hear one overhead, I’ll notice it right away, and sometimes my chest tightens before I’ve even really thought about it. It’s not like I’m sitting there deciding to be scared, it’s just this immediate reaction.

And with planning, even something as normal as looking up flights for a conference can set it off really fast. I’ll be okay, and then I see the flight options or picture actually being on the plane, and I get this rush of panic where I feel like I need to shut the laptop or get away from the whole thought. It feels kind of ridiculous because nothing is actually happening yet, but my body reacts like it is.
When you're not thinking about flying or hearing planes, do you find yourself feeling unusually on edge, easily startled, or having trouble relaxing in general?

Um… I don’t think so, not in a general way. Like, if there’s nothing about flying coming up and I’m not hearing a plane or looking at travel stuff, I don’t usually feel like I’m walking around constantly on edge.

I mean, I have normal stress, like anyone does, especially with work and daily responsibilities, but I haven’t really noticed being unusually jumpy or unable to relax all the time. It feels more like that reaction is tied pretty specifically to planes or the idea of flying, rather than just being there in the background all day.
Do you find yourself having intrusive thoughts, flashbacks, or vivid memories of that turbulent flight from your honeymoon, even when you're not thinking about flying?

Um… not really, no. I mean, I remember the flight if something brings it up, like if someone mentions bad turbulence or I’m thinking about booking a flight, but I don’t think I’m just randomly getting flashbacks out of nowhere.

It’s more like the memory is there and it’s unpleasant when I go back to it, but I’m not, like, suddenly transported back to the plane while I’m making dinner or sitting at work or anything like that. I don’t really have vivid scenes popping into my head unless I’m already thinking about flying in some way. So… I guess I’d say no, not when there’s nothing reminding me of it.
Do you ever find yourself avoiding other situations or activities because of fear or anxiety, even if they aren’t related to flying?

I don’t think so… not really. I’m trying to think of examples, because I guess everyone avoids things sometimes if they’re stressful or inconvenient, but I can’t think of other situations where fear kind of makes the decision for me the way flying does.

Like, I don’t avoid going places in general, or meetings, or driving, or being around people because I’m anxious. If something isn’t connected to flying, I usually just do it, even if I’m nervous or it’s not my favorite thing. So no, I haven’t really noticed that happening with other activities. It feels pretty specific.

When you're reminded of flying or think about it, do you find yourself having negative thoughts about the situation, like feeling like you won’t be able to cope or that something terrible will happen?

Yeah… I do. Not all the time, but when flying comes up, my mind goes pretty quickly to, “What if I can’t handle it?” or “What if something goes wrong?” Even just picturing myself getting on the plane can make me feel like it’s going to be unbearable.

And I know, logically, people fly every single day and most flights are completely fine. I can say that out loud and I do believe it, in a rational way. But emotionally it’s like my brain skips over that and goes right back to that honeymoon flight with the turbulence. I start picturing the plane dropping or shaking, and then I imagine myself trapped there, not able to get off, just panicking or waiting for something terrible to happen.

So yes, I think the negative thoughts are a big part of it. It’s not just “I don’t like flying.” It’s more like flying has started to feel way scarier than it should, and my mind kind of fills in the worst-case scenario before I can talk myself down.
Do you find that your anxiety about flying lingers even after you're no longer directly thinking about it, like being unable to shake the worry even when you're doing other things?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I don’t think it lingers in the sense that I’m anxious all day afterward or I can’t function once the thought passes. Usually if something reminds me of flying, I’ll get that rush of worry and I might think about it for a bit, especially if there’s an actual trip or possibility of a trip involved.

But if it’s just, like, a commercial with an airplane or someone casually mentioning travel, I can usually move on once the moment passes. I might feel a little unsettled for a few minutes, but I don’t think I’m walking around hours later still consumed by it.

If I’m actively dealing with planning a flight, then it’s harder to shake, because there are decisions attached to it and I keep circling back to it. But otherwise… no, I haven’t really noticed the worry sticking around when I’m focused on other things.
Do you ever find yourself avoiding places, activities, or even conversations that are related to flying—like airports, travel planning, or talking about trips—even if you don’t have to actually fly?

Yes… I think I do, actually. I was going to say it’s only the actual flying part, but when I really think about it, I avoid a lot of the things around it too.

Like if there’s a work training or conference that would involve flying, I’ll start looking for reasons not to go, or I’ll ask if there’s a virtual option, or I’ll just turn it down if I can. And for trips where flying would make the most sense, I’ve pushed for driving instead, even when it’s a really long drive and kind of unreasonable. I’ll frame it like, “Oh, it’ll be nice to have the car,” or “We can make it a road trip,” but honestly a big part of it is that I’m trying to avoid getting on a plane.

Even conversations about planning trips can make me want to shut down. If my husband and I have to talk about flights or dates or airports, I really need him sitting with me and kind of keeping me steady, because otherwise I start finding excuses to stop the conversation or say, “Let’s talk about it later,” and then I just don’t come back to it. It’s embarrassing, because it’s not like I’m even at the airport in that moment, but just having to seriously talk about a trip makes me feel like I’m going to back out.
Do you find yourself avoiding even looking at travel websites, airline apps, or anything else that might remind you of flying, even when there’s no immediate need to plan a trip?

Yeah… I think so, at least indirectly. I don’t know if I’d say I’m constantly avoiding travel websites just for no reason, like if there’s truly nothing coming up I’m not usually browsing them anyway. But if something even starts to become a real possibility, I can feel myself wanting to not look. Like I’ll put off opening the airline site or checking flight times because once I do, it makes the whole thing feel real.

And honestly, that’s kind of the pattern I’ve gotten into. I’ll choose these really long drives instead of flying, even when flying would clearly make more sense. Or with work trainings, if I know flying would be involved, I’ve turned them down or looked for some way around it. I tell myself it’s practical or that I’m too busy, but I know the flying part is a big reason.

If I absolutely have to talk through a trip, I usually need my husband sitting there with me. Not because he’s doing anything complicated, just… having him there keeps me from spiraling into “I can’t do this” and backing out of the conversation completely. If I’m by myself, I’m much more likely to close the tab, say I’ll deal with it later, and then avoid it.

No definitive features to exclude any of these at this point.

This turn ruled out PTSD (F43.10) due to absence of intrusive thoughts, flashbacks, or dissociative reactions unrelated to flight-related stimuli. The anxiety remains situation-specific (flying), supporting specific phobia (F40.20) or panic disorder with agoraphobia (F40.10) as remaining candidates.

Not because he’s doing anything complicated, just… having him there keeps me from spiraling into “I can’t do this” and backing out of the conversation completely. If I’m by myself, I’m much more likely to close the tab, say I’ll deal with it later, and then avoid it.
